scenes.visual: Title card 'One Budget, Many Uses'. COLOUR MAP, the same in both films and on the page: BLACK bar = intake (A), what one animal takes in; GOLD = reproduction (R); TEAL = self (S: growth, upkeep, storage, drawn as teal sub-bands when split out); GREY = trend lines and labels. Axes, when shown: horizontal = GOLD reproduction R, vertical = TEAL self S. The songbird is the same small great-tit-like cartoon in both films; the salmon icon matches the lesson's semelparity figure. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Cartoons and labelled blocks only, no molecular structures; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A salmon swims upriver, spawns once, and dies. A songbird nests every spring for years. Both are shaped by natural selection. So how can both strategies be right?
scenes.visual: Split screen. Top: a salmon icon swims along a horizontal lifeline, a single GOLD reproduction marker appears, and the line ends just after it. Bottom: the songbird's lifeline runs on, with a GOLD marker added each spring (spring labels tick by). A large grey question mark fades in between the two lines.
scenes.narration: A salmon swims upriver, spawns once, and dies. A songbird nests every spring for years. Both are shaped by natural selection. So how can both strategies be right?

scenes.tts: Start with one bird in one season. Treat what it takes in and can use as one fixed budget. That budget must pay for four uses. Growth. Upkeep, meaning maintenance and repair. Storage. And reproduction.
scenes.visual: The songbird pecks at seeds; a BLACK bar labelled 'intake (A): one budget, schematic' fills beneath it. As each use is named, the bar splits into four bands left to right: 'growth', 'upkeep (maintenance and repair)', 'storage' in three TEAL shades, and 'reproduction' in GOLD. The four bands always add up to the full black bar's length. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Start with one bird in one season. Treat what it takes in and can use as one fixed budget. That budget must pay for four uses. Growth. Upkeep, meaning maintenance and repair. Storage. And reproduction.

scenes.tts: Lump the first three together as self, in teal. Reproduction stays gold. For this one bird, gold plus teal always equals the intake. So more gold means less teal. That negative link is a trade-off.
scenes.visual: The three TEAL bands merge into one TEAL band 'self (S)'. On screen: 'R + S = A'. Axes appear: GOLD 'reproduction R' horizontal, TEAL 'self S' vertical. A straight line runs from A on the vertical axis to A on the horizontal axis (slope -1), labelled 'trade-off line'. A slider under the bar moves the gold/teal split; a dot slides along the line in step, the gold band growing as the teal band shrinks.
scenes.narration: Lump the first three together as self, in teal. Reproduction stays gold. For this one bird, gold plus teal always equals the intake. So more gold means less teal. That negative link is a trade-off.

scenes.tts: Two classic trade-offs live on this line. First, current against future reproduction: what a parent spends on this year's young is not spent on itself. Second, number against size of offspring. A fixed amount put into a clutch can make many small eggs, or a few large ones.
scenes.visual: Label 1 slides onto the line: 'this year's young (GOLD) vs parent's own upkeep and future (TEAL)'. Then the GOLD band lifts off as a 'clutch' bar and is cut first into eight small eggs, then re-cut into three large eggs of the same total length. Label 2: 'many small or few large'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Two classic trade-offs live on this line. First, current against future reproduction: what a parent spends on this year's young is not spent on itself. Second, number against size of offspring. A fixed amount put into a clutch can make many small eggs, or a few large ones.

scenes.tts: Picture two birds with the same intake. One pours most of it into this year's brood. The other keeps more for itself. Each sits at one point on the line, its split. Selection acts on that split. It favours whichever split leaves the most descendants. Which split wins depends on who dies at what age.
scenes.visual: Two songbirds on the same trade-off line: one dot near the GOLD end, one near the middle. From each dot a lifeline runs forward a few seasons with GOLD markers; small chick icons stack up under each as 'descendants'. Caption 'selection acts on the split'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Picture two birds with the same intake. One pours most of it into this year's brood. The other keeps more for itself. Each sits at one point on the line, its split. Selection acts on that split. It favours whichever split leaves the most descendants. Which split wins depends on who dies at what age.

scenes.tts: Picture two worlds. In the first, adults rarely survive the winter, but their young survive well. In the second, adults usually survive, while many young die, or their survival swings from year to year.
scenes.visual: Two panels. 'World 1': a snowflake passes; most adult bird icons fade out, chick icons stay bright. Label 'adult survival p: low', 'young survival c: high'. 'World 2': adults stay bright through the snowflake; chick icons flicker and many fade, and a 'young survival' bar bounces up and down year by year. Label 'p: high', 'c: low or variable'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Picture two worlds. In the first, adults rarely survive the winter, but their young survive well. In the second, adults usually survive, while many young die, or their survival swings from year to year.

scenes.tts: Here is a question for you. In the first world, adults rarely live to breed again. Does that lower or raise the extra young one big bout needs to pay?
scenes.visual: World 1 panel enlarged, its trade-off line beside it with the dot in the middle and a pulsing question mark over the slider.
scenes.narration: Here is a question for you. In the first world, adults rarely live to breed again. Does that lower or raise the extra young one big bout needs to pay?

scenes.visual: Hold on the World 1 panel and question mark; a small 5-second ring timer counts down.

scenes.tts: It lowers it. Holding back buys a future that rarely comes. So putting more into this year's bout can pay, as in the salmon. How far still depends on how extra effort changes breeding and survival. In the second world, teal buys more breeding seasons. Holding back to breed again can pay, as in the songbird.
scenes.visual: World 1: a small 'extra young needed' bar shrinks; the dot slides well toward the GOLD end of the line but stops short of the end (label 'how far: set by the trade-off's shape, schematic'), and the salmon lifeline from the opening lights up. World 2: the dot slides toward TEAL and the songbird lifeline lights up, its GOLD markers repeating spring after spring.
scenes.narration: It lowers it. Holding back buys a future that rarely comes. So putting more into this year's bout can pay, as in the salmon. How far still depends on how extra effort changes breeding and survival. In the second world, teal buys more breeding seasons. Holding back to breed again can pay, as in the songbird.

scenes.tts: That is why no organism can grow fast, breed early, make many large offspring and live long all at once. Salmon and songbird follow one rule in different worlds. One intake, one split. Selection picks the split that leaves the most descendants where that animal lives.
scenes.visual: The two lifelines slide together under a single BLACK intake bar with its GOLD/TEAL split; the salmon's slider sits near the gold end, the songbird's nearer the middle. Caption: 'same rule, different worlds'.
scenes.narration: That is why no organism can grow fast, breed early, make many large offspring and live long all at once. Salmon and songbird follow one rule in different worlds. One intake, one split. Selection picks the split that leaves the most descendants where that animal lives.

scenes.tts: There is one catch. So far every bird had the same intake. Real animals do not all take in the same amount. Hold that thought, because it changes what real data show.
scenes.visual: A second songbird appears with a much longer BLACK intake bar beside the first; its trade-off line sits further out from the corner, parallel to the first. A grey question mark hovers between the two lines.
scenes.narration: There is one catch. So far every bird had the same intake. Real animals do not all take in the same amount. Hold that thought, because it changes what real data show.

scenes.visual: End card with the hexagon mascot: 'Selection picks the split leaving most descendants, given who dies when.'
